\begin{abstract} An agent with long-term memory can answer from a record it should no longer use, such as a plan the user later cancelled. We test whether an agent can tell, before retrieving anything, that its store holds such a record, from a summary alone: the number of records in each lifecycle state, and a list of attribute names with the values removed. Each of 148 questions is asked against three versions of one store that differ in one attribute, so a question's wording cannot give the answer away. First, ablations show that the two smaller of five models rely on the attribute names alone, while the three stronger ones also use the state counts. Second, for superseded records, the one state whose names the summary lists, no model reliably beats a cosine-similarity lookup over those names. Under a control that holds counts and list length fixed, the lookup and every model pick the correct name over a similar one at an AUROC of 0.88 or higher (chance 0.50). The stronger models lead the lookup by 0.08 to 0.10 overall, a lead that comes from retracted and expired records, which the summary only counts; adding one count feature to the lookup closes it. Third, the memory backends we tested omit or misstate this information. Given only what FR-Bank, a backend that tags every entry with a lifecycle state, actually writes, GPT-4.1 mini and the lookup drop from 0.73 and 0.75 to 0.60 and 0.59 on our larger question set. In these tests, what the store wrote down mattered more than which model read it. All stores are synthetic, and whether better judgments yield better answers is not established; human validation is pending. \end{abstract}
